activities.caption: file the claims: reliability or validity
activities.name: psyReliabilityBuckets

config.prompt: Reliability or validity? File each claim under the standard it belongs to:
buckets: reliability — does it agree with itself?
validity — does it support the interpretation?

items.label: same people, same test, weeks apart — temporal stability
Cronbach's alpha: effectively the average inter-item correlation
ten reworded versions of one bad question reach alpha near 0.95
do the items sample the domain they claim to?
do scores predict a real outcome — concurrently or predictively?
convergent correlations with related measures, discriminant non-correlations with unrelated ones

config.why: An unreliable measure cannot be valid — validity is bounded by the square root of reliability — but high reliability is cheap and says nothing about validity.

config.prompt: A reported IQ of 124 on this test (reliability 0.90, SD 15) carries a 95% band of 124 ± 9. Place the marker at the band's lower edge:
config.why: SEM = 15 × √0.10 ≈ 4.7 points, so two SEMs ≈ 9 and the honest band runs from about 115 to 133 — which is why a four-point difference between two children's scores on a good test is noise.

activities.anchor: an exact quantity like a height in centimetres
activities.caption: find the faulty line — a score report
activities.name: psyExactSpot

config.prompt: One line of this score report's interpretation is wrong — click it:
lines: A reported IQ of 124 means the person's intelligence is exactly 124, like a height in centimetres.
The score is an estimate with a band: on a good test, 124 is honestly about 115 to 133 at 95% confidence.
The same child retested next month may land several points either way.
Professional practice reports confidence intervals because the band, not the point estimate, carries decision weight.
config.correction: A reported score is an estimate with an error band — treating point scores as exact attributes is how four-point differences between applicants get mistaken for real differences in ability.
config.why: The SEM, not the point estimate, carries the decision weight.

activities.caption: pair the facets and the traps
activities.name: psyValidityMatch

config.prompt: Pair each validity facet — and each named trap — with its description:

pairs.right: do the items sample the domain? an exam that is all arithmetic lacks it for maths
do scores predict a real outcome — concurrently or predictively?
convergent with related measures, discriminant against unrelated ones
validating a job test against supervisor ratings when supervisors know the scores
rebranding reliable instruments as new constructs — the 'emotional intelligence' cautionary tale

config.why: Validity is not a property a test has; it is the strength of evidence that scores support a particular interpretation — the multitrait-multimethod matrix is the classic design.

activities.caption: which curve matches g at work?
activities.name: psyManifoldTrace

config.prompt: Meta-analysis finds g predicts job performance at r ≈ 0.5 overall. Which curve matches how that validity behaves as job complexity rises?

curves.label: validity rises as job complexity increases
validity falls as job complexity increases
validity is flat across job complexity

config.why: Meta-analytic r ≈ 0.5, rising with job complexity — and g-loading rises with subtests' abstractness. The interpretive claims (one biological efficiency? van der Maas's mutualism? sampling of learned skills?) remain the field's live frontier.

activities.anchor: a partition that could be computed per individual
activities.caption: true or false — the heritability misreading
activities.name: psyHeritJudge

statements.s: 'Heritability of 0.8' means 80% of a person's intelligence came from their genes and 20% from their environment.
statements.why: Heritability is a population statistic — the share of variation between people in a particular environment attributable to genetic differences; no such split exists for one person.

statements.s: Make the environment more equal and heritability rises; make it wildly unequal and it falls.
statements.why: Which is how a trait can be strongly heritable and still shift thirty points in three generations, as the Flynn effect showed.

statements.s: Heritability within a population constrains how much the trait can change between environments.
statements.why: It constrains nothing of the sort — the standard misreading this course exists to kill.

statements.s: High heritability and the Flynn effect can both be true at once.
statements.why: Twin estimates around 0.5 in childhood and 0.7–0.8 in adulthood in WEIRD samples sit alongside massive environmental malleability across cohorts, plus family-environment effects in adoption studies.

activities.anchor: A modern standardised test is engineered end-to-end
activities.caption: order the life of a test
activities.name: psyTestLifeOrder

config.prompt: From blueprint to score report — order the pipeline:
items: A test blueprint specifies content domains and cognitive levels; items are sampled to match
Items are written, bias-reviewed and pretested on representative samples — misbehaving items are discarded invisibly
Scaling and equating place raw scores on the reported scale, IRT anchoring new forms to old ones
Reliability is estimated from the operational data — alpha, or IRT information functions that quantify precision at each ability level
Expert panels set the cut scores by documented methods — Angoff, Bookmark
The score report carries standard-error bands and interpretation guidance
config.why: The statistics standardise, the standard is human: the judgement content of the cut-score step is the dirty secret of every certification exam, and communicating precision honestly is the professionals' first duty.

activities.anchor: The consequences are everywhere in modern testing
activities.caption: walk an adaptive test, item by item
activities.name: psyAdaptiveBranch

config.root: You are sitting a computerised adaptive test (the GRE's adaptive sections). Your ability estimate sits at theta, mid-scale.

start.text: The next item appears. You answer it correctly. What does the algorithm do?

choices.label: Selects a harder item at your raised estimate
choices.feedback: The estimate rises and the next item targets it — precision is quantified at each ability level, the refinement classical reliability misses.

choices.label: Stops the test — you have passed
choices.feedback: Not yet: the test runs until your estimate is precise enough, which is how it halves test length at equal precision.

mid.text: A harder item follows, and this one you miss. What happens to the estimate — and to the next item?

choices.label: The estimate eases down; an easier item follows
choices.feedback: Each item's own response function — a logistic curve of ability with difficulty, discrimination and guessing parameters — updates the estimate item by item.

choices.label: The estimate crashes; the test restarts from zero
choices.feedback: No restarts: where classical theory treats every item equally, IRT tracks the estimate continuously.

end.text: The test ends when your estimate is precise enough — half the length, equal precision; equating across forms and years becomes principled, and item banks can be audited for differential item functioning at scale.

config.why: Item response theory replaced the classical toolkit: the item bank, the estimate and the next-item choice are all running off each item's own response function.
